https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89: Russian ship engulfed in flames after explosion at Libyan port
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."

If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.

As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.

But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj75: Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3d: How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg: Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.
Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added.
Watch: Moment Mexican reporter takes cover on air as gunshots ring out nearby
Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.
Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.

The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.
It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.
When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was arrested

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e3: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media. , external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.

Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.

Chairman and CEO of LVMH, Bernard Arnault - who is one of the world's richest people - offered his condolences and also paid tribute to Paolo Bulgari.

In 2019, Paolo Bulgari and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwe9: George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6wy: Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

He has just returned from helping communities devastated by the deadly flash floods - more than a decade after doing the same following the earthquakes there.

He admits to The Detail that it was a harrowing and heartbreaking trek back to his home country, which began five days after the flash floods hit on 26 August, and finished just a couple of weeks ago.
"We lost so many people... almost 400 people that I personally knew, and so every day was a funeral ritual," he says.
"So for 49 days I was just attending one funeral after another, and sometimes in a day...10 to 15 funeral rituals.
"Sometimes it was for an individual, sometimes a group. Sometimes it's communal with... 52 people. So, I was on a wave of funeral rituals.

"It's a very roller coaster time because all of a sudden you feel happy to see all the surviving people... you kind of feel 'oh, they survived', but then as you talk to them you also realise that so many people that you know are not going to come back."
In Nepal, more than 1400 people were killed, while more than 5200 remain missing.
In Tibet, 43 people died, with more than 500 on the missing list. Some victims were swept 250 kilometres into neighbouring India.

"Our village is completely obliterated, completely destroyed, now completely a floodplain - just a barren rock. Nothing exists there. Just from my home village, we lost 181 locals - mostly close relatives and friends... no one survived... during this disaster.

"When I saw my hometown... I didn't even realise that my eyes were full of tears and... my body was super cold and it was shivering, and then my friend gave me a hug, and then I realised... how bad it is."
Sunil's hometown, Syaphru Besi, in 2011 (L) and after the 2026 floods (R).
Tsunami-like walls of water destroyed the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border and struck dozens of settlements along a 72 km stretch of the Trishuli River on the morning of 26 August.
But nearly three months on, rebuilding has not been straightforward. Some of the houses Tamang rebuilt after the 2015 earthquakes can not be fixed this time round.
"We lost houses then, but we still had the land, so we could go back and somehow managed to rebuild. But now we don't have the land.
"And in some areas, it is completely unsafe. There is no possibility to rebuild there. That is the reality now, at least in my part of the village - I don't think that's possible."
"I think there is a need for the government to figure out some kind of solution with very, very close consultation with the local community.
"It's not just about losing your people, but you are also losing a place that holds so much to you... and being an indigenous community, this is really, really important."
He says about US$5 billion is required for the reconstruction recovery, but "we don't have that money - that's almost 10 percent of GDP for Nepal".
"We have got a lot of sympathies and support - emotional support - from international communities, but we also need to materialise this... with real help on the ground."

New Zealand was ready to support a draft deal that prompted UN climate talks to collapse without a decision.
COP31 ended on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, with no consensus after more than two weeks of fraught negotiations.
The final draft deal, known as a cover decision, avoided any mention of the fossil fuels driving global warming.
The European Union, together with Panama and several other countries, formally objected to the draft, saying it was "unconscionable" to support it.
A spokesperson for New Zealand's caretaker climate minister, Simon Watts, said New Zealand was "ready to support a consensus on the cover decision".
Asked to confirm if that meant New Zealand supported the final draft as it stood, the spokesperson said: "Yes - New Zealand would have supported consensus in the room."

Despite the lack of a decision, the conference - which Watts attended for three days last week - was "a valuable opportunity for New Zealand to engage internationally and strengthen important relationships", the spokesperson said.
Green MP Francisco Hernandez, who was at COP31 until this morning NZT, said the EU and others were right to reject the draft decision.
The lack of any language about a transition away from fossil fuels was especially disappointing, he said.

"That was probably the most egregious thing for us - not naming fossil fuel as the thing that's causing climate change is basically like going to a cancer conference and not acknowledging smoking as the cause of lung cancer," he said.
The language about finance to assist vulnerable countries to adapt to climate change was also too weak, he said.
"There were some positive things in the text - things like the electrification target of 35 percent by 2035 - but unfortunately there was no real language there that it had to be clean energy."
The EU and others were right to walk away from the deal, he said.
"The draft text was just so weak - it doesn't meet the moment."
There were rumours all weekend that the deal would not pass, and a "febrile" atmosphere among the negotiating teams.
The failure to agree in a cover decision did not mean COP31 itself had failed, he said.
"I think people would be remiss to come away ... with the impression that we need to do less on climate, not more... This COP failed because it wasn't ambitious enough."
However, there was "probably merit" in considering whether the format of climate COPs - particularly the requirement for consensus decision-making - needed a second look.

"It really doesn't make sense to allow a small group of fossil fuel producers to hold the rest of the world hostage... Saudi Arabia was quite aggressive in trying to block progress on any of the texts."

He was a highly influential figure in Australia's music industry as a critic, producer, interviewer and television presenter.
Australian Molly Meldrum, the former host of Countdown, has died aged 83.
For decades, if Meldrum urged viewers to "do yourself a favour" and buy your record, you knew you had made it in the music business.
Meldrum was a highly influential figure in Australia's music industry as a critic, producer, interviewer and television presenter.
As the host of Countdown, Molly Meldrum held extraordinary sway over what music Australian young people listened to.
The sold-out show at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena was held to raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia, following Farnham’s own health battle in 2022.
‘You're The Voice’ is bigger than a pop song: the unofficial anthem still inspires singalongs at pubs, stadiums and festival fields decades later.
Rose Tattoo frontman Angry Anderson has died just weeks after being admitted to a hospital in Germany during the Australian rock band's European tour.

As the host of the ABC's music show Countdown, he brought the world's biggest pop stars into people's homes, and recorded some of the most iconic — if sometimes chaotic — interviews ever broadcast on Australian television.

Instantly recognisable in his trademark cowboy hat, Meldrum was described by some as "the most important person in pop", whose influence on the chart success of performers — particularly Australians — could not be overstated.
The ABC spoke to a close friend of Molly Meldrum's who said he had been in a Melbourne hospital for a number of days before dying.
Ian "Molly" Meldrum was born in Orbost, in regional Victoria, on January 29, 1943.
He spent the first 10 years of his life in the small country town before moving to the even smaller country town of Quambatook to live with his grandmother.
"My grandmother was one of my biggest influences on my life and I lived a fair bit with her and I absolutely adored my grandmother," he said.
"She taught me one of the great things that I've tried to live my life by and she told me that no-one's above you and no-one's below you and you should treat all people as equal."
Meldrum's interest in music surged when The Beatles toured Australia in 1964, taking the country by storm.
Meldrum and his friend Ronnie Burns — who would later have a successful recording career of his own — were kicked out of The Beatles' concert in Melbourne for being "too enthusiastic".

Just a few years later, Meldrum, who had been writing for Go-Set magazine and working on local TV shows, relocated to London to document Australian band The Groop's attempts to crack the UK music scene.
It was there that he got the scoop that took his career to a new level, securing an interview with John Lennon during which the Beatle dropped the bombshell that the band was splitting up.
"The story later went worldwide on radio, in Rolling Stone, everywhere," Meldrum said in 1981.
Meldrum had also been learning the ropes as a music producer, assisting with the recording of music by artists such as The Masters Apprentices.
Molly Meldrum worked as a reporter for Go-Set magazine in the 1960s and 1970s.
In 1969 he produced Russell Morris's recording of The Real Thing, transforming the song, which was written by Johnny Young as an acoustic ballad, into a six-minute, effects-laden epic.
The song was a number one hit domestically and is widely regarded as a milestone in music production in Australia.
Meldrum had experience as a television music reporter, but taking a job with brand new ABC music show Countdown was to be the single most important move in his career.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment_c: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment_climate/2734804%2Fcop-flop-scientist-warns-countries-are-losing-faith-in-un-climate-summits-as-deal-talks-stall
A climate scientist warns COP31 risks being seen as "a flop".
A New Zealand climate scientist says many countries are losing faith in the UN's annual climate summits, with the deal at COP31 teetering on collapse.
He said Pacific Island nations were among those who were deeply frustrated with this year's summit, as they face an "existential threat" of 1.5 degrees of global warming .
Fraught negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye have run more than a day over deadline, with international publications reporting a major deadlock overnight.
Talks stalled when a draft of the deal contained no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels, The Guardian reported.
EU, Pacific Island and African states were pushing for the wording, while Saudi Arabia was among those understood to be pushing against it.
Then, at a late-night session, COP31 presidents Australia and Türkiye announced a new package aimed at achieving consensus.
President Murat Kurum said he believed concerns around fossil fuel wording had been solved, as had those around providing funding developing countries' climate change adaptation programmes.
"I truly remain hopeful, I still believe that we can arrive at some excellent decisions here in this hall, here in Antalya.
"The gap between us is narrowing, and the political will required to build a bridge exists right here in this room," he told the BBC.
A third draft of the deal has been sent to delegates in the early hours of the morning.

COP31 had been dubbed the "Implementation COP", with a focus on action for climate change financing and adaptation, Victoria University's Professor of Earth Sciences Tim Naish, who attended the summit as Chair of the World Climate Research Programme, said.
Instead, it had been one of the least productive ever and would be a failure if no deal was reached.
"It was a given that we would continue this so-called roadmap of transitioning away from fossil fuels that people thought wouldn't be controversial.
"What can happen at this COP is, essentially it's a flop, and we don't get any traction on the core goals that were set going into this process."

Naish said even if a deal was reached, he did not expect it to be transformative as the summit had "backslid" on major issues. Meanwhile, the world was getting closer to the Paris Agreement target of 1.5C degrees of warming , he added.
He said Pacific Island nations, who had a very strong voice at COP, were especially frustrated.
Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown addresses leaders at PRECOP31 discussions in Fiji.
"This is why they are at the COP, 1.5 degrees is existential for them."

One of the world's biggest polluters, the United States, was not there, and climate change was getting less public attention amidst other major geopolitical issues and a general sense the 1.5 degrees target couldn't be reached.

"Bottom line is I think people are losing faith in the process, they are not seeing the process working, but I think the majority would be very loathe to leave it, because it's all we've got at the moment."

Karan Titus, a researcher in renewable energy engineering at the University of Canterbury who also attended COP31, said lack of pathways for climate adaptation finance had been a big weakness in the negotiations up till now.

Titus said he thought carbon capture and storage was being used as a way to solve the fossil fuel wording deadlock, but in his view this technology risked lock-in of fossil fuel projects for many years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jr: The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.
Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.
The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.
"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".
The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.
Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.
Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.

The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.
The government has said some households will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget .
The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.
But consumer groups have argued the £100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.
Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter.
"For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."
The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies.
"Our inflated energy prices are driven by inflated energy firm profits," the group said.
"Government and Ofgem must take stronger action against this blatant profiteering whilst we suffer in cold homes, or are forced into debt."
Energy firms operating in the UK are subject to a windfall tax that was introduced in 2022.
When the windfall tax is added to other taxes levied, it means the overall tax rate on profits earned by oil and gas companies operating in the UK is 78%.
